subtitle: Eighteen chapters, one battlefield, and the question of how to act

sections.label: Orientation
sections.title: Before We Begin
sections.subtitle: The battlefield, the three lenses, and how to read a text that has been read for two thousand years

blocks.html: Seven hundred verses. Two men in a chariot, stopped in the empty ground between two armies that are about to destroy each other. One of them will not fight. The other will spend the next eighteen chapters explaining why he must — and in the course of explaining, will hand the world one of the most examined arguments ever made about how a human being should act.

blocks.name: lenses
blocks.caption: The same three lenses, applied to a text that has been read for two thousand years.

blocks.html: That is the Bhagavad Gita — bhagavad-gītā, "the song of the Blessed One." It is not a standalone scripture. It is an episode inside the Mahabharata, the enormous Sanskrit epic of roughly one hundred thousand verses that tells how a single royal family tore itself apart. The Gita is a conversation that happens on the morning of the war, and it lasts, in the story's own time, only as long as two armies are willing to stand still and wait.
The Family That Could Not Divide a Kingdom

You need only the bones of the epic. The Kuru dynasty has two branches. Dhritarashtra, blind from birth, has a hundred sons — the Kauravas, eldest of them Duryodhana. His late brother Pandu has five — the Pandavas: Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva. The cousins grow up in one household and quarrel over one throne. Duryodhana rigs a dice game; the Pandavas lose their kingdom and their freedom, and their wife Draupadi is humiliated in the assembly hall while the elders sit silent. Thirteen years of exile follow. On their return Yudhishthira asks not for the kingdom but for five villages, and Duryodhana refuses to yield land enough to fit under the point of a needle.

So both sides call in every ally they have, and the armies meet at Kurukshetra. Almost everyone Arjuna loves is standing on the other side: his grand-uncle Bhishma who raised him, his teacher Drona who made him the archer he is, cousins, friends, the men he grew up beside. This is the situation into which the Gita drops. It is not a philosophical seminar. It is a nervous breakdown on a battlefield, and the philosophy is the emergency response.
Who Is Arjuna? Who Is Krishna?

Arjuna is the third Pandava and the finest archer alive — disciplined, celebrated, the man who never loses. He is also the one who thinks. The epic gives its collapse to its most competent character, which is precisely why it works: the Gita is not addressed to the weak but to the capable person who suddenly cannot see why any of it matters.

Krishna is a Yadava prince of Dvaraka, cousin and lifelong friend to Arjuna, and cousin also to the Kauravas. Approached by both sides before the war, he made an offer that tells you everything about him: one side could have his armies, the other could have him alone, unarmed, refusing to lift a weapon. Duryodhana took the armies. Arjuna took Krishna — who became his sārathi, his charioteer, holding the reins at the front of the vehicle while the archer stands behind. In the theology of the text he is far more than a cousin: he is an avatāra of Vishnu, and in the eleventh chapter he stops speaking as a friend and shows Arjuna what he actually is. Hold both. The Gita's force comes from the fact that the driver of the chariot turns out to be the ground of being — and is still, in chapter eighteen, your friend.
Where the Gita Sits

The Mahabharata is divided into eighteen books, called parvans. The sixth is the Bhishma Parva, the book of the first ten days of fighting. The Gita occupies eighteen chapters near the start of it — numbered 23 to 40 in the Pune critical edition, 25 to 42 in the older vulgate, which is your first small lesson in how texts actually reach us. It has been extracted, printed and taught on its own for centuries, but it was written to be read where it stands: as the thing that happens just before the arrows start.
The Three Lenses
One promise before we start. This course will never let one kind of truth wear another's clothes. Everything here belongs to exactly one of three registers, and you will always be told which:

items.title: Scriptural / Mythological
items.html: What the text actually says, on its own terms — Krishna's arguments, Arjuna's objections, the narrative of the epic around them. Taken seriously as what it is, without translating it into something else first.

items.title: Symbolic / Philosophical
items.html: What the tradition and its commentators understand the text to mean — the chariot as the body, the war as the inner conflict, karma-yoga as a psychology of action. Read as a key is read: it opens the lock of experience, or it doesn't.

items.title: Historical / Scholarly
items.html: What textual criticism, manuscript evidence and academic study can reasonably establish — when it was likely composed, how it was likely assembled, who has read it which way and why. True the way a verdict is true: beyond reasonable doubt, always appealable.

blocks.html: These do not compete. A verse can be historically late, symbolically inexhaustible and devotionally alive at once. Collapse the lenses one way and you get fundamentalism — myth mistaken for a police report. Collapse them the other way and you get the flat cynicism that thinks calling something "just a story" is an argument. Keep them apart and you get understanding.

blocks.tag: Practice · How to Read This Course

blocks.html: Eighteen chapters, eighteen sittings — that is the traditional pace, and it is a good one. Read one chapter section here, then read that chapter of the Gita itself in any translation you like, and notice where the translator has made a choice. Do not try to agree with the text on the first pass. The Gita survived two thousand years of argument because it rewards argument; readers who fought with it — Shankara, Ramanuja, Tilak, Gandhi — got more out of it than readers who nodded.

Before you learn anything: write down, in one sentence, what you currently think the Gita is about. Most people write some version of "do your duty without expecting results." Keep the paper. At the end of chapter eighteen, read it again — not to find out whether you were wrong, but to see how much larger the same sentence has become.
Throughout, verse citations follow the standard chapter.verse numbering (2.47 = chapter two, verse forty-seven). Where editions genuinely differ — and in chapter thirteen they do — you will be told.

sections.label: Stage 01 · Context
sections.title: The War Before the Verse
sections.subtitle: How eighteen days of war produced eighteen chapters of philosophy

blocks.html: Every teaching has a situation that produced it, and the Gita is unusually honest about its own. Nothing in it is asked in the abstract. Arjuna is not curious about the nature of the self; he is standing between two armies with his bow slipping out of his hands, and the questions come out of him in the order that panic produces them.
Eighteen Days at Kurukshetra

The war lasts eighteen days. Bhishma commands the Kaurava army for ten of them and falls on a bed of arrows; Drona commands for five; Karna for two; Shalya for the last. Nearly everyone dies. The Pandavas win a kingdom emptied of the people they wanted to rule it with, and the epic spends its final books on the aftertaste — Yudhishthira's grief, Gandhari's curse, Krishna's own clan destroying itself in a drunken brawl, and the five brothers walking north into the Himalayas to die. The Gita sits inside that catastrophe like a still point. The epic is not triumphalist; it is one of world literature's longest arguments about the cost of being right.
The Blind King and the Man Given Sight

Now notice how the text reaches you, because it matters. Dhritarashtra is blind. He cannot watch the war his refusal to restrain his son has caused. So the sage Vyasa offers him the divya-cakṣus, the divine eye, to see the battle himself. He declines — he does not want to watch his sons die — and asks that the gift be given instead to Sanjaya, his charioteer and bard, who will sit beside him in the palace and narrate.

So every word Krishna speaks reaches us at a distance. Sanjaya, sitting miles away, describes to a blind king what a god is saying to a warrior. And Sanjaya's narration is itself being recited by Vaishampayana to King Janamejaya, which is itself being recited by the bard Ugrashrava to a gathering of sages in the Naimisha forest. Four nested frames, and the Gita's very first word is spoken by a blind man asking what is happening.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The first verse of the Gita
blocks.sk:
धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः ।
मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय ॥
blocks.tr: dharma-kṣetre kuru-kṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ / māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāś caiva kim akurvata sañjaya
blocks.mn: "On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered together and eager to fight — what did they do, my sons and the sons of Pandu, O Sanjaya?"

blocks.tag: Symbolic Lens · Two names for one field

blocks.html: The commentators have never let go of that opening line. The same ground is named twice in a single breath: dharma-kṣetra, the field of righteousness, and kuru-kṣetra, the field of the Kurus — the family field, the field of inheritance and grievance. Every place we are asked to act is both at once: a moral arena and a mess of history we did not choose. And note who is speaking. Dhritarashtra says māmakāḥ — "mine" — for one set of nephews and "the sons of Pandu" for the other. The war is already contained in that pronoun. A tradition-minded reader will also point out that the Gita opens on the word dharma and closes, seven hundred verses later, on the word mama — "mine." Dharma... mama. My duty. The text is a bracket around a single phrase.
How Old Is It?

Here we change lenses, and you should feel the gear-shift. Everything above is the story as the story tells itself. What follows is what evidence can support — which is less, and less precise, than either devotional or debunking accounts usually admit.

The scholarly consensus, such as it is, places the Gita's core somewhere in the broad window of the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE. Some serious scholars argue for earlier — the 4th or 3rd century BCE; others for a somewhat later crystallisation. The Mahabharata as a whole is later still in its final form, generally described as having taken shape over roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE, layered by many hands. The Gita therefore sits inside a text that was still growing around it.

Why the vagueness? Because there is no external anchor. No inscription mentions the Gita in its first centuries. No datable manuscript survives from anywhere near its composition — Indian manuscript traditions on palm leaf and birch bark rarely preserve copies more than a few hundred years old, and our oldest Gita manuscripts postdate the text by a very long way. Dating is done indirectly: by language, by metre, by which philosophical vocabulary the text does and does not know, and by its relationship to Buddhist and early Samkhya thought.

The honest sentence is this: we know the Gita is old; we do not know how old. Anyone who hands you a single year — 3102 BCE or 150 CE — is selling a certainty the evidence cannot buy. This does not make the text less serious. It makes the people who study it more so.
What the Gita Is Made Of

The text is a weave of at least three earlier currents, and one pleasure of reading it closely is watching the seams. From Samkhya it takes the analysis of reality into puruṣa (consciousness) and prakṛti (matter-and-mind), and the three guṇas. From Yoga it takes discipline, breath, posture, the steadying of attention. From the Upanishads it takes the deathless self, ātman, and its relation to brahman. And then it does something none of its sources quite did: it fuses all three onto a personal God who can be loved, and insists the whole apparatus is meant to be used in the middle of your life, not after you have left it.

That last move is the Gita's actual innovation, and it explains its afterlife. Renunciation was the prestige option in its world: the serious seeker left. The Gita says the serious seeker stays, does the work in front of him, and changes his relationship to it instead. Every reader who has had to be good inside a job, a family, a war, or a country has found the text waiting for them.

sections.label: Chapter 01 · Arjuna Viṣāda Yoga
sections.title: Arjuna's Despair
sections.subtitle: The only scripture in the world that opens with its hero having a breakdown

blocks.html: Chapter one is almost entirely a list. Conches are named, warriors are named, formations are described, and then Arjuna asks Krishna to drive the chariot into the space between the armies so he can see who he has come to kill. He looks. And the chapter, which has been building like a war film, collapses inward into the body of one man.

What Arjuna reports is a panic attack described with clinical accuracy: his limbs give way, his mouth dries, his body trembles, his hair stands on end, his skin burns, his mind reels, and Gandiva — the great bow, the instrument of his identity — slips from his hand. He cannot stand up. He does not say I am afraid; he says he can see no good in killing his own people, that victory would be worthless, that the destruction of a family destroys its ancient dharma and the survivors fall into chaos. Then he sits down on the floor of the chariot, in the middle of the battlefield, and puts his weapons away.

blocks.sk:
एवमुक्त्वार्जुनः सङ्ख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत् ।
विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः ॥
blocks.tr: evam uktvārjunaḥ saṅkhye rathopastha upāviśat / visṛjya saśaraṁ cāpaṁ śoka-saṁvigna-mānasaḥ
blocks.mn: "Having spoken thus, in the midst of the battle Arjuna sank down upon the seat of the chariot, casting away his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief."
blocks.src: — Bhagavad Gita 1.47 (1.46 in editions that count the speaker-lines differently)

blocks.html: Why the Text Needs Him to Fall

Notice what the Gita has done structurally. It has spent an entire chapter establishing Arjuna's competence — the conches, the ranks, the reputation — before removing it. A teaching about detachment delivered to someone with nothing to lose would be cheap. Delivered to the best warrior on the field, at the moment his whole life's training arrives at an act he cannot perform, it costs something. The Gita's teacher does not begin until the student has genuinely run out.

And Arjuna's argument is good. This is the part most summaries skip. He is not being cowardly and the text never says he is; his stated case is a moral one, made in the vocabulary of dharma itself — kin-slaying pollutes, family collapse corrupts the women, corrupted lineage ends the ancestral rites, and the whole social order unravels. He reasons his way to paralysis. That is why chapter two cannot answer him with sentiment. It has to go underneath the argument entirely.

The image was already old when the Gita used it. The Katha Upanishad gives the classic version: the body is the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) is the charioteer, the mind is the reins, the senses are the horses, and the self is the passenger who owns the ride but does not drive it. The Gita puts Krishna in the driver's seat — which, read symbolically, is the whole teaching in one picture. The crisis is not that the horses are wild. The crisis is who is holding the reins. Arjuna's despair begins the moment he asks to be positioned where he can see, and it ends only when he agrees to let someone else steer.

The traditional name of the chapter is viṣāda-yoga — "the yoga of despair." Sit with that construction. The tradition did not call it the chapter of Arjuna's failure. It called his collapse a yoga: a discipline, a joining, a legitimate way in. Whatever else the Gita is, it is a text that thinks breakdown can be a doorway rather than a disqualification.

sections.label: Chapter 02 · Sāṅkhya Yoga
sections.title: The Yoga of Discernment
sections.subtitle: The whole Gita in miniature — the deathless self, the discipline of action, and the mind that has stopped shaking

blocks.html: If you only ever read one chapter, read this one. Chapter two contains, in compressed form, nearly everything the remaining sixteen will unpack: the argument from the imperishable self, the doctrine of acting without attachment to results, the ladder by which desire becomes destruction, and the portrait of the person whose wisdom has become stable. Many scholars think it is also the oldest core of the text. Certainly it reads like the seed from which the rest grew.

It opens with Krishna refusing to be kind. Arjuna says plainly that he will not fight, and calls Krishna his student, asking to be taught. Krishna's first words as a teacher are a rebuke: aśocyān anvaśocas tvaṁ prajñā-vādāṁś ca bhāṣase — "you grieve for those who should not be grieved for, and you speak the language of wisdom while doing it" (2.11). The wise, he says, mourn neither the living nor the dead. Then he begins.
The First Argument: What Cannot Be Killed

Krishna's opening move is metaphysical. There has never been a time when you were not, nor these kings; nor will any of us cease to be. As a person passes through childhood, youth and age within one body, so the embodied one passes into another body — and the steady are not disturbed by this. The self, ātman, is not a thing that happens to living beings; it is what is looking out of them.

blocks.sk:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्
नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो
न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
blocks.tr: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin / nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ / ajo nityaḥ śāśvato 'yaṁ purāṇo / na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre
blocks.mn: "It is never born and it never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient — it is not slain when the body is slain."

blocks.tag: Scriptural Lens · The four elements cannot touch it

blocks.html: Three verses later comes the line every Sanskrit student learns early:

blocks.sk:
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः ।
न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः ॥
blocks.tr: nainaṁ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṁ dahati pāvakaḥ / na cainaṁ kledayanty āpo na śoṣayati mārutaḥ
blocks.mn: "Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, wind does not dry it."

blocks.html: Note the rhetorical precision of the list on a battlefield: the four things that destroy bodies in a war — the blade, the pyre, the flood, the exposure — are named one by one and declared powerless. The verse is not a general metaphysical statement. It is an answer aimed exactly at what Arjuna is afraid of.

It is worth being honest about how this argument lands on a modern reader. Krishna is telling a man not to grieve killing because the essential person cannot be killed. If you do not already accept an imperishable self, the consolation does not transfer — and the text does not pretend otherwise. Krishna himself seems to know it is not enough, because he immediately changes tack: even if you think the self is repeatedly born and repeatedly dies, he says at 2.26, you still should not grieve, since what is born must die and what dies must be born. Two arguments, one metaphysical and one simply about the terms of existence, offered in sequence to a man who is not persuaded by either.
The Second Argument: The Famous One

From verse 39 the chapter turns, and Krishna announces that he has given Arjuna the reasoning of Samkhya and will now give him the reasoning of yoga — meaning, here, a discipline of action. What follows is the single most quoted verse in Hindu literature.

blocks.sk:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
blocks.tr: karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana / mā karma-phala-hetur bhūr mā te saṅgo 'stv akarmaṇi
blocks.mn: "Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruits of action be your motive; and do not be attached to inaction either."

blocks.html: Read the fourth line, because it is the one that gets dropped. Mā te saṅgo 'stv akarmaṇi — do not be attached to inaction. The verse is not a licence for passivity or a spiritual excuse for not caring how things turn out. It is a precise instrument with two blades: one cuts the grip of outcomes on your motivation, the other cuts the temptation to withdraw. What is left is action performed at full strength with the anxiety removed from it. Krishna gives it a name in the next verse, and the name is a definition worth memorising: samatvaṁ yoga ucyate — "evenness of mind is what is called yoga" (2.48).
The Ladder Down

The chapter closes with a portrait of the sthita-prajña, the one whose insight is steady — a figure Arjuna asks about directly at 2.54, in the Gita's first genuinely eager question. How does such a person speak, sit, walk? Krishna's answer runs to the end of the chapter, and inside it is a two-verse mechanism of psychological decay that has probably been quoted more often in Indian ethical writing than any other passage.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · How a person is destroyed
blocks.sk:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते ।
सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
क्रोधाद्भवति सम्मोहः सम्मोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः ।
स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥
blocks.tr: dhyāyato viṣayān puṁsaḥ saṅgas teṣūpajāyate / saṅgāt sañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho 'bhijāyate / krodhād bhavati sammohaḥ sammohāt smṛti-vibhramaḥ / smṛti-bhraṁśād buddhi-nāśo buddhi-nāśāt praṇaśyati
blocks.mn: "Dwelling on objects, a person becomes attached to them; from attachment desire is born; from desire, anger. From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from confusion of memory, the destruction of discernment — and when discernment is destroyed, the person is lost."

blocks.html: Seven steps from idle attention to ruin, and each link is observable in an ordinary week. Note that the sequence begins with dhyāyataḥ, "dwelling on" — not with the object and not with the desire, but with the mind's decision to keep circling something. That is the point at which intervention is cheap. By the time you are at anger, the rest of the ladder is nearly automatic.

And the chapter's closing image answers Arjuna's question about the steady person with something better than a rule. Desires enter such a person, Krishna says (2.70), as rivers enter the ocean — which is filled and yet unmoved, holding its own level. Not a person without desire. A person large enough that desire no longer determines the tide.

Test 2.47 against one real thing this week — a piece of work, a conversation, an application, a difficult message you have to send. Do it as well as you can and deliberately release the result before you know it. Then notice what happens to the quality of the doing. Most people report the same surprising thing: the work gets better, not worse. That observation is not proof of anything metaphysical, but it is data, and it is yours.

sections.label: Chapter 03 · Karma Yoga
sections.title: The Yoga of Action
sections.subtitle: Nobody gets to stop — so the question is never whether to act, only how

blocks.html: Arjuna opens chapter three with an entirely reasonable complaint. If understanding is better than action, he asks, why are you pushing me into this appalling deed? Krishna's answer sets the direction of the rest of the text: because nobody, not for a single instant, actually stops.

No one can remain even for a moment without acting, Krishna says; everyone is made to act, helplessly, by the qualities born of nature (3.5). And the one who sits still while the mind runs after objects of sense is not a renunciate but a hypocrite — mithyācāra (3.6). Withdrawal is not an available option; it is only a differently packaged action, usually a worse one. The chapter therefore reframes Arjuna's entire question. He thinks he is choosing between fighting and not fighting. He is choosing between two kinds of doing.
Sacrifice as a Model of Everything

To explain how action can be done without binding, Krishna reaches for the oldest institution in his culture: yajña, Vedic sacrifice. Along with living beings, he says, the creator emitted sacrifice, and told them to prosper by it — you nourish the gods, the gods nourish you, and by that mutual nourishment all thrive (3.10–3.11). The world is a circulation. Whoever eats without contributing to the cycle is described bluntly as a thief (3.12).

This is a decisive move, made quietly. The Gita takes sacrifice — a technical ritual of fire, mantra and priests — and generalises it into a structure of consciousness. Any act done as offering rather than acquisition is a yajña. The kitchen, the desk and the battlefield are all altars, depending entirely on the direction the act is facing. Everything Karma Yoga becomes in later Indian thought is contained in that generalisation.

blocks.sk:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् ।
स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥
blocks.tr: śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt sv-anuṣṭhitāt / sva-dharme nidhanaṁ śreyaḥ para-dharmo bhayāvahaḥ
blocks.mn: "Better one's own duty imperfectly done than another's duty done well. Better to die in one's own duty; another's duty brings danger."

blocks.html: This verse has done enormous work in Indian history, in both directions. Read one way it is a liberating instruction against imitation: do your own work badly rather than someone else's brilliantly, because a borrowed life, however successful, has no traction on your actual situation. Read another way — and it was read this way for centuries — svadharma means the duty assigned by birth, and the verse becomes a defence of a caste order in which you should stay where you were placed. Both readings are genuinely in the text's reception history. Pretending otherwise, in either direction, is not honesty.
Janaka, and the Argument from Consequence

Krishna adds a second reason to act, and it is social rather than personal. Janaka and others attained perfection precisely through action (3.20); and beyond that, one should act for loka-saṅgraha — the holding-together of the world (3.20–3.25). Whatever a great person does, others do; the standard they set is the one the world follows (3.21). Krishna then applies it to himself: there is nothing in the three worlds he needs to obtain, nothing unattained he must attain — and still he works, because if he stopped, everything would follow him into collapse.

So the fully liberated person keeps working, not from need but from position. This is the Gita's answer to the perennial suspicion that spiritual attainment is a form of quitting. The freer you get, the more of the world's weight you can carry without being crushed by it, and therefore the more of it you should carry.

blocks.tag: Practice · Turning an act into an offering

blocks.html: The technique the chapter implies is small enough to actually do. Before one ordinary task today — cooking, answering email, a meeting you resent — pause for one breath and mentally hand the result away. Not "I don't care how this goes," which is a lie, but "this is offered." Then work at full effort. The Gita's claim is that these two things, total effort and released outcome, are compatible; most of us have never tested whether that is true, because we assume caring about the result is what generates the effort. The chapter says the anxiety and the effort are separable, and that the anxiety was never doing the work you thought it was.

The chapter ends with Arjuna asking the question any honest reader has been holding: what is it that drives a person to do wrong, even against his own will, as if by force? Krishna names it in one word — kāma, desire, and its shadow anger, born of rajas, the great devourer, the great enemy here (3.37). Not a devil, not fate: an appetite lodged in the senses, the mind and the intellect, which veils knowledge as smoke veils fire, dust veils a mirror, the womb veils an embryo (3.38). Three images of concealment in ascending density — and the point of all three is that nothing has been destroyed. It has only been covered.

sections.label: Chapter 04 · Jñāna Karma Sannyāsa Yoga
sections.title: Knowledge, Action, and Renunciation
sections.subtitle: Krishna reveals that he has been here before — and defines action so strangely that it becomes stillness

blocks.html: Chapter four begins with a claim about transmission: this imperishable yoga was told to Vivasvat, who told Manu, who told Ikshvaku, and so it came down through the royal sages until it was lost by long lapse of time. Arjuna, sensibly, objects. Vivasvat was born long ago; you were born recently. How am I to understand that you taught it at the beginning?

Krishna's answer is the first moment in the Gita where he steps entirely out of the role of friend and charioteer. Many births of mine have passed, and of yours too; I know them all, you do not. Though unborn and imperishable, though lord of beings, he says, he takes birth through his own power, by his own māyā — and then comes the promise on which an entire theology rests.

blocks.sk:
यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत ।
अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥
परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् ।
धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
blocks.tr: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata / abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham / paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām / dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge
blocks.mn: "Whenever there is a decline of dharma, O Bharata, and a rising up of adharma, then I send forth myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of wrongdoers, for the firm establishing of dharma, I come into being age after age."

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · Where avatāra comes from

blocks.html: These two verses are the classical charter of the avatāra doctrine — the idea that Vishnu descends into the world in successive forms. Scholars generally regard the Gita as an early and important witness to that idea rather than its complete formulation: the standardised list of ten avataras, with Krishna in a fixed slot, belongs to later Puranic literature, not here. What the Gita gives is the principle and the reason, not the roster.

A related historical note belongs with this chapter. At 4.13 Krishna says the fourfold order — cāturvarṇya — was created by him "according to the distribution of qualities and actions" (guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśaḥ). Commentators have fought over that phrase for a thousand years, because it can be read as grounding social class in innate quality and work rather than in birth, and reformers from the nineteenth century onward pressed exactly that reading. It can equally be read as divine sanction for the order as it stood. The Sanskrit permits both; the historical record shows both were used. Note also that Krishna's very next clause disowns authorship in the ordinary sense — "know me to be the non-doer" — which complicates any straightforward appeal to the verse as legislation.
Action in Inaction
The chapter's philosophical heart is a deliberate paradox. Even poets are confused about what action and inaction are, Krishna says; and then:

blocks.sk:
कर्मण्यकर्म यः पश्येदकर्मणि च कर्म यः ।
स बुद्धिमान्मनुष्येषु स युक्तः कृत्स्नकर्मकृत् ॥
blocks.tr: karmaṇy akarma yaḥ paśyed akarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ / sa buddhimān manuṣyeṣu sa yuktaḥ kṛtsna-karma-kṛt
blocks.mn: "The one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction — that one is wise among men, disciplined, and has done all that is to be done."

blocks.html: This is not wordplay. It is the recognition that the visible surface of behaviour tells you nothing about whether binding is occurring. A person can sit motionless in a cave and be furiously entangled; a person can conduct a war and be untouched. What determines the difference is the presence or absence of the sense of being the doer, grasping at a result. Krishna's own description of such a person is worth having: he has abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, is always content, dependent on nothing, and though fully engaged in work, he does nothing at all (4.20).

The rest of the chapter catalogues the many forms of yajña that seekers practise — offering the senses into the fires of restraint, offering breath into breath, offering wealth, austerity, study — and then ranks them: the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to any material sacrifice, because all action without exception is completed in knowledge (4.33). And it ends with the most quoted instruction in Indian pedagogy.

blocks.sk:
तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया ।
उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः ॥
blocks.tr: tad viddhi praṇipātena paripraśnena sevayā / upadekṣyanti te jñānaṁ jñāninas tattva-darśinaḥ
blocks.mn: "Know this by prostration, by inquiry, by service. Those who know, who see into the truth of things, will teach you knowledge."

blocks.html: Three conditions, and the middle one is the surprise. Praṇipāta — humility, the bowed head. Sevā — service, doing something useful for the person who teaches you. But between them sits paripraśna: persistent questioning, asking around a thing until it opens. The tradition did not ask for belief. It asked for humility and interrogation in the same gesture, which is a harder combination than either alone, and a fair description of what this entire course is trying to do.

sections.label: Chapter 05 · Karma Sannyāsa Yoga
sections.title: Renunciation and Action
sections.subtitle: Arjuna asks Krishna to finally pick one — and gets told the two were never different

blocks.html: Arjuna is losing patience, and it is a relief to see it. You praise the renunciation of actions, he says, and then you praise yoga — tell me definitely which one is better (5.1). Any reader of the previous three chapters has wanted to ask exactly that. Krishna's reply is that both lead to the highest good, but that of the two, the yoga of action is the better — and then he spends the chapter dissolving the distinction Arjuna was asking about.

The reason the question is malformed is that sannyāsa — renunciation — is being used in two senses. If it means giving up activity, it is a change of circumstance and does not touch the problem. If it means giving up the inner claim on results, it is identical with karma yoga and requires no change of circumstance at all. Krishna states it flatly: the one who neither hates nor craves is to be known as a permanent renunciate, free from the pairs of opposites, easily released from bondage (5.3). Children speak of Samkhya and yoga as different, he says; the learned do not. Whoever sees one sees both (5.4–5.5).

blocks.sk:
ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः ।
लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा ॥
blocks.tr: brahmaṇy ādhāya karmāṇi saṅgaṁ tyaktvā karoti yaḥ / lipyate na sa pāpena padma-patram ivāmbhasā
blocks.mn: "One who acts, placing all actions in Brahman and abandoning attachment, is not stained by evil — as a lotus leaf is untouched by water."

blocks.tag: Symbolic Lens · Why a lotus leaf, and not a stone

blocks.html: The image is chosen with care, and it is not the image of invulnerability. A stone is unwetted because it is dense and closed. A lotus leaf is thin, alive, permeable to light, and it lies on the water, in continuous contact with it — and the water still beads and runs off. The tradition's ideal of non-attachment is the leaf, not the stone: maximum contact, minimum absorption. Anyone who has met the cold, armoured version of "detachment" that people sometimes bring back from spiritual books has met a stone claiming to be a leaf. The Gita's word for the leaf's quality is anāsakti, and Gandhi thought it so central that he named his entire commentary after it.
The City of Nine Gates

Krishna offers a striking image for the embodied self: renouncing all actions by the mind, the dweller sits happily in the city of nine gates — nava-dvāre pure — neither acting nor causing action (5.13). Nine gates: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two lower openings. The body as a walled town with nine points of exchange with the world, and the self as its resident rather than its machinery. It is a picture of embodiment without identification — you live here; you are not the masonry.
From this follows one of the Gita's most ethically radical verses, and one that sits in genuine tension with other parts of the text.

blocks.sk:
विद्याविनयसम्पन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि ।
शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः ॥
blocks.tr: vidyā-vinaya-sampanne brāhmaṇe gavi hastini / śuni caiva śva-pāke ca paṇḍitāḥ sama-darśinaḥ
blocks.mn: "In a brahmin endowed with learning and humility, in a cow, in an elephant, and even in a dog and in an outcaste who cooks dog — the wise see the same."

blocks.html: The verse deliberately spans the full social and biological range its audience could imagine, from the most honoured human being to the most degraded, and asserts that the seeing that matters does not register the difference. It has been quoted by every Indian social reformer who worked inside the tradition rather than against it. It also sits, unresolved, beside 4.13's fourfold order and 9.32's ranking of who may reach the highest goal. The Gita is not systematically egalitarian, and it is not systematically hierarchical. It contains both, and the tradition's readers have had to choose which verse interprets which — which is exactly what a living text is.

The chapter ends by turning toward meditation, and so hands off cleanly to chapter six: shutting out external contacts, fixing the gaze between the brows, balancing the breath, the sage who has made desire, fear and anger fall away is forever free (5.27–5.28). And the last verse gives the reason it works — knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all worlds, the friend of all beings, one attains peace (5.29). Suhṛdaṁ sarva-bhūtānām. The universe, in the Gita's view, is not neutral toward you.

sections.label: Chapter 06 · Dhyāna Yoga
sections.title: The Yoga of Meditation
sections.subtitle: Posture, breath, the lamp in a windless place, and the kindest promise in the text

blocks.html: Chapter six is the Gita's practical manual, and the only place in it where you are told what to do with your body. Choose a clean spot, neither too high nor too low, spread cloth and grass; sit there, hold the body, head and neck erect and still, gaze steady, mind quiet, and practise. It is also, unexpectedly, the most tender chapter in the book — because it is the one that deals with failure.

It opens by continuing chapter five's argument: the true renunciate is the one who does the work that must be done without depending on its fruit, not the one who has merely stopped lighting the ritual fire (6.1). Then it turns inward with a verse that has become a standing instruction in every Indian self-help tradition since.

blocks.sk:
उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् ।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
blocks.tr: uddhared ātmanātmānaṁ nātmānam avasādayet / ātmaiva hy ātmano bandhur ātmaiva ripur ātmanaḥ
blocks.mn: "Let one lift oneself by oneself; let one not degrade oneself. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is its enemy."

blocks.html: The Sanskrit is a deliberate hall of mirrors — ātman appears in nearly every position in both lines — and the ambiguity is the meaning. Which self lifts which? The next verse answers: the self is the friend of one who has conquered the self by the self, and hostile to the one who has not. There is no third party in this transaction. The Gita is unusual among devotional texts in insisting, right in the middle of a book about surrendering to God, that the work of self-mastery is not outsourced.
The Middle Way of the Body

The instructions are notably moderate, and the moderation is deliberate. Yoga is not for one who eats too much or eats nothing at all, sleeps too much or stays awake too long. For one whose food, recreation, effort, sleeping and waking are measured, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow (6.16–6.17). In a culture with a long and honoured tradition of extreme asceticism, this is a considered rejection of heroics. The person who tortures the body is not, by the Gita's lights, further along.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The classic simile for a steady mind
blocks.sk:
यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता ।
योगिनो यतचित्तस्य युञ्जतो योगमात्मनः ॥
blocks.tr: yathā dīpo nivāta-stho neṅgate sopamā smṛtā / yogino yata-cittasya yuñjato yogam ātmanaḥ
blocks.mn: "As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker — that is the traditional simile for the yogi of controlled mind, practising union with the self."

blocks.html: And in this state the yogi sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, seeing the same everywhere (6.29) — which the chapter then converts into an ethical criterion at 6.32 that is easy to skip past and very hard to live: the highest yogi is the one who, by analogy with the self, sees the same everywhere, whether in pleasure or in pain. Not the one who has the most refined internal states. The one whose regard for others' pain has become structurally identical to his regard for his own.
"The Mind Is Restless, Krishna"

Then Arjuna interrupts with the most human line in the chapter. This yoga of evenness you describe — I do not see its steady foundation, because the mind is unsteady (6.33). The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful, obstinate; I think it as hard to hold as the wind (6.34). Krishna does not deny it. Without doubt, mighty-armed, the mind is hard to restrain and restless — but, he says, it is held by practice and by dispassion: abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate (6.35). Two words, one meaning repetition over time, the other meaning a loosened grip. No shortcut is offered, then or since.

blocks.tag: Practice · What the chapter actually asks

blocks.html: Ten minutes. A clean spot, a steady seat, spine upright without strain, gaze soft or closed. Follow the breath. When the mind goes — and it will go, in seconds, and again in seconds — bring it back without commentary. Krishna's instruction at 6.26 is exactly this and nothing more elaborate: wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off to, from there restrain it and bring it back under the control of the self. Not "stop it wandering." The wandering is assumed. The practice is the return, and the practice is the return again.

The chapter closes with Arjuna's real fear, which is not about technique. What happens, he asks, to the one who tries this, fails, and dies unfulfilled — does he perish like a torn cloud, fallen from both worlds, with no ground under him at all (6.37–6.38)? Krishna's answer is the sentence that has kept a great many people practising:

blocks.sk:
पार्थ नैवेह नामुत्र विनाशस्तस्य विद्यते ।
न हि कल्याणकृत्कश्चिद्दुर्गतिं तात गच्छति ॥
blocks.tr: pārtha naiveha nāmutra vināśas tasya vidyate / na hi kalyāṇa-kṛt kaścid durgatiṁ tāta gacchati
blocks.mn: "O Partha, neither here nor hereafter is there destruction for him. No one who does good, my son, ever comes to a bad end."

blocks.html: Hear the word tāta — "my son," "dear one" — from a cousin the same age, spoken on a battlefield. It is the only place in the Gita where Krishna talks like that. The unfinished practice, he goes on, is not lost: such a person is reborn in favourable circumstances and picks up the thread, drawn on by the practice of the previous life even against his will (6.43–6.44). Whatever you make of rebirth — and we look at it honestly in the final section — the psychological instruction is clear. Effort is cumulative. Nothing sincere is wasted. Begin again.

sections.label: Chapter 07 · Jñāna Vijñāna Yoga
sections.title: Knowledge and Realisation
sections.subtitle: The Gita changes key — from what you should do to who is holding the reins

blocks.html: Chapters one through six are, broadly, about you: your duty, your action, your mind, your discipline. From chapter seven the subject changes. Krishna begins speaking about himself, and the remaining twelve chapters are increasingly the answer to a question Arjuna has not yet asked — who exactly is talking to me?

He begins with a distinction the chapter is named for. Jñāna is knowledge; vijñāna is the realisation of it, knowledge that has become experience — I will declare to you this knowledge together with its realisation, knowing which nothing further remains to be known here (7.2). Then a piece of honesty rare in a scripture: among thousands of people, scarcely one strives for perfection; and among those who strive and succeed, scarcely one knows me in truth (7.3). The Gita does not oversell its own accessibility. It will spend chapters nine and twelve making it far more accessible than this verse suggests — but it starts by admitting the difficulty.
The Lower and Higher Natures

Krishna divides his own nature into two. The lower, eightfold: earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and I-sense — the whole apparatus of the material and mental world. And the higher: the very life-principle by which this universe is sustained (7.4–7.5). All beings, he says, have their origin in these two. Then he says he is the origin of the whole world and its dissolution too, and gives the chapter's central image.

blocks.sk:
मत्तः परतरं नान्यत्किञ्चिदस्ति धनञ्जय ।
मयि सर्वमिदं प्रोतं सूत्रे मणिगणा इव ॥
blocks.tr: mattaḥ parataraṁ nānyat kiñcid asti dhanañjaya / mayi sarvam idaṁ protaṁ sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva
blocks.mn: "There is nothing whatever higher than me, O Dhananjaya. All this is strung upon me like clusters of gems upon a thread."

blocks.html: The simile repays a moment. The gems are what you see; the thread is what you do not. Remove the thread and the necklace is not damaged, it simply ceases to be a necklace — a heap of separate beautiful things with no relation. What Krishna claims to be is not the largest gem. He is the continuity, the fact that these things constitute an order at all. And the verses that follow apply it concretely and rather beautifully: I am the taste in water, the light in the moon and the sun, the sound in ether, the manliness in men, the pure fragrance of the earth, the brilliance in fire, the life in all beings, the austerity in ascetics (7.8–7.9). Not the water, the taste of it. Not the fire, its brightness. He is naming himself as the quality that makes each thing itself.
Four Kinds of People Who Turn Toward God

At 7.16 comes a classification that has shaped Indian devotional literature ever since. Four kinds of virtuous people worship me, Krishna says: ārta, the distressed; jijñāsu, the one who wants to know; arthārthī, the one who wants something; and jñānī, the one who knows. What is remarkable is that the list is not a rebuke. Three of the four come with an agenda — pain, curiosity, need — and all four are called virtuous. The tradition read this as permission: you do not have to purify your motive before you begin. You are allowed to arrive at the door for the wrong reason.
Krishna does state a preference — of these, the one steadily established in knowledge is dearest, and he calls that person his own self (7.17–7.18). And then, at the end of a long road:

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · At the end of many births
blocks.sk:
बहूनां जन्मनामन्ते ज्ञानवान्मां प्रपद्यते ।
वासुदेवः सर्वमिति स महात्मा सुदुर्लभः ॥
blocks.tr: bahūnāṁ janmanām ante jñānavān māṁ prapadyate / vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti sa mahātmā su-durlabhaḥ
blocks.mn: "At the end of many births, the one who knows takes refuge in me, realising that Vasudeva is all. Such a great soul is very hard to find."

blocks.html: Which of the four are you? Be accurate rather than flattering — most sincere readers arrive as some mixture of ārta and jijñāsu, distress and curiosity, and are slightly ashamed of the first. The chapter says you need not be. But notice, too, what the fourth kind is not doing: the jñānī has no petition. Ask yourself honestly what you would still want from a practice if it were guaranteed to change nothing in your circumstances. Whatever remains in the answer is the part of you that is already past the transaction.

The chapter ends by explaining why so few see it. Deluded by the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion, beings are born into confusion (7.27); and Krishna is veiled by his own yoga-māyā, so the world does not recognise him (7.25). Note the asymmetry the rest of the text depends on: he knows all beings, past, present and to come — but no one knows me (7.26). Chapter eleven is the moment that sentence stops being true, and Arjuna will wish it had stayed true.

sections.label: Chapter 08 · Akṣara Brahma Yoga
sections.title: The Imperishable Absolute
sections.subtitle: Cosmic time, the last thought, and the door out of the cycle

blocks.html: Arjuna opens chapter eight with a burst of seven technical questions — what is Brahman, what is the self, what is action, what is the domain of the elements, of the divine, of sacrifice, and how are you to be known at the time of death? Krishna answers each in a compressed verse or two, and then settles on the last one, because it is the one that matters to a man who expects to die tomorrow.

blocks.sk:
यं यं वापि स्मरन्भावं त्यजत्यन्ते कलेवरम् ।
तं तमेवैति कौन्तेय सदा तद्भावभावितः ॥
blocks.tr: yaṁ yaṁ vāpi smaran bhāvaṁ tyajaty ante kalevaram / taṁ tam evaiti kaunteya sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ
blocks.mn: "Whatever state of being one remembers when one leaves the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kunti, having always been absorbed in it."

blocks.html: Read the last four words carefully, because they prevent the verse from being a superstition. Sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ: "always made-to-become by dwelling in that state." The final thought is not a lottery ticket you can buy at the last second; it is a summary. What surfaces when everything else is being stripped away is whatever has been rehearsed longest. Krishna's practical instruction follows immediately and is entirely consistent — therefore remember me at all times, and fight (8.7). Not "remember me at the end." The end takes care of itself if the middle has been attended to.

blocks.tag: Story · Bhishma on the bed of arrows

blocks.html: This chapter's teaching has a famous illustration a few books later in the same epic. Bhishma, the Kuru patriarch, falls on the tenth day of the war, pierced by so many of Arjuna's arrows that he never touches the ground — the shafts hold him above it. He had been granted the boon of choosing the hour of his own death, and he chooses to wait: the sun is in its southern course, and he will not go until it turns north. So he lies on that bed of arrows for weeks, conscious, and spends the time teaching — the long discourses on dharma and liberation that make up two of the Mahabharata's largest books. Read against 8.6 the scene is almost programmatic: the dying man's final months are filled entirely with the thing he wants to be dwelling in when he goes.

The Gita itself distinguishes two departures at 8.24–8.26 — the bright path of fire, light, day and the northern course of the sun, from which there is no return, and the dark path of smoke, night and the southern course, from which one comes back. Historically, these two paths are inherited: they appear in the Upanishads before the Gita, as the devayāna and pitṛyāna, the way of the gods and the way of the ancestors. The Gita takes an older cosmological map and folds it into its own argument.
A Day of Brahma
Then the chapter opens out into deep time, and the scale is worth pausing on.

blocks.sk:
सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः ।
रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ॥
blocks.tr: sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ / rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te 'ho-rātra-vido janāḥ
blocks.mn: "Those who know that a day of Brahma lasts a thousand ages, and that his night also ends after a thousand ages — those people know day and night."

blocks.html: At the coming of Brahma's day, all manifest beings stream out of the unmanifest; at the coming of his night, they dissolve back into it. The same multitude, helplessly, again and again (8.18–8.19). This is the Indian cosmological picture at its most characteristic: not one creation and one end, but respiration — a universe that breathes in and out over spans of time so long that human history does not register. And beyond even that periodic dissolution, Krishna says, there is another unmanifest, eternal, which is not destroyed when all beings are destroyed (8.20). That is the akṣara, the imperishable, that gives the chapter its name and is called the highest goal.

It is worth naming the emotional function of a passage like this, because it is easy to read it as mere cosmological trivia. Arjuna is frozen by the enormity of what one day will do to his family. Chapter eight sets that day inside a duration in which entire universes are a single exhalation. This is either the coldest thing in the Gita or the most consoling, and different readers have honestly reported both.

sections.label: Chapter 09 · Rāja Vidyā Rāja Guhya Yoga
sections.title: The Royal Knowledge, the Royal Secret
sections.subtitle: The chapter where the door is thrown open to absolutely everyone

blocks.html: Chapter nine calls itself the king of knowledge and the king of secrets, and then reveals something that turns out to be less a secret than an invitation. It is the emotional centre of the Gita's devotional teaching, and it contains verses that were quietly revolutionary in their social setting.

It begins with a paradox stated flatly. All this world is pervaded by me in unmanifest form; all beings dwell in me, and I do not dwell in them (9.4). And then, immediately: and yet beings do not dwell in me — behold my sovereign yoga (9.5). Commentators have worked on that contradiction for centuries. The most common reading: things depend on him as waves depend on the sea, but he is not contained by them or affected by them; the containment runs one way only. Krishna calls his own formulation an expression of aiśvaram yogam, sovereign mystery, rather than resolving it. The Gita is content to leave certain seams visible.

blocks.sk:
अनन्याश्चिन्तयन्तो मां ये जनाः पर्युपासते ।
तेषां नित्याभियुक्तानां योगक्षेमं वहाम्यहम् ॥
blocks.tr: ananyāś cintayanto māṁ ye janāḥ paryupāsate / teṣāṁ nityābhiyuktānāṁ yoga-kṣemaṁ vahāmy aham
blocks.mn: "Those who worship me with undivided attention, thinking of no other — for them, ever steadfast, I carry what they lack and preserve what they have."

blocks.html: Yoga-kṣema is a single compound with a concrete history: yoga here means acquisition, getting what one does not have; kṣema means safekeeping, holding what one has. It is the vocabulary of a householder, not a mystic. The verse promises the two things every anxious person actually wants, and the verb is vahāmi — "I carry." It is recited at shop openings and before journeys across India, and one can see why.

blocks.tag: Scriptural Lens · A leaf, a flower, a fruit, water

blocks.sk:
पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति ।
तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः ॥
blocks.tr: patraṁ puṣpaṁ phalaṁ toyaṁ yo me bhaktyā prayacchati / tad ahaṁ bhakty-upahṛtam aśnāmi prayatātmanaḥ
blocks.mn: "Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water — that offering of devotion, from one whose heart is pure, I accept."

blocks.html: Consider what this verse does to a religious economy built on expensive sacrifice. A leaf. Water. The four cheapest things on earth, available to anyone with hands, requiring no priest, no fire, no fee, no ritual qualification. The operative word is bhaktyā — "with devotion" — which is the only currency named, and it cannot be taxed. Krishna then generalises it in the next verse: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give away, whatever austerity you practise, do it as an offering to me (9.27). The entire apparatus of religion is compressed into an orientation of attention, and then handed to everyone.
Even the Worst Person

At 9.29 Krishna says he is the same in all beings — none hateful to him, none dear — but those who worship him with devotion are in him and he in them. And then comes a verse that made the later devotional movements possible: api cet su-durācāro bhajate mām ananya-bhāk — even if a person of very bad conduct worships me with undivided heart, he is to be regarded as good, for he has rightly resolved (9.30). He swiftly becomes righteous and attains lasting peace; know for certain, Arjuna, that my devotee never perishes (9.31). Not "will be forgiven eventually." Is to be regarded as good, now, by you.

And then 9.32, which needs to be handled with both hands. Those who take refuge in me, Krishna says, even if they are of "sinful birth" — pāpa-yonayaḥ — women, vaishyas, and shudras, even they attain the highest goal. Read forward, this is the door being opened: the highest attainment is declared available to precisely the groups excluded from Vedic study and ritual, and the bhakti traditions of the following millennium walked through that door in enormous numbers. Read closely, the premise is demeaning: the categories are grouped under a phrase about inferior birth, women among them, and the concession is framed as remarkable. Both things are in the verse. Reformers have leaned on the first half; critics have pointed at the second; some traditional commentators have argued the phrase attaches only to the first category and not to the list. The historically honest statement is that the Gita is, on this question, a text of its time doing something unusual for its time — and that neither half of that sentence cancels the other.

The chapter closes with the instruction that the whole devotional tradition took as its charter: fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow to me; so shall you come to me, having made me your highest goal (9.34). Krishna will repeat this sentence, almost word for word, as the final teaching of the entire book at 18.65 — which tells you that in the Gita's own architecture, this chapter is not a detour on the way to something more sophisticated. It is the destination.

sections.label: Chapter 10 · Vibhūti Yoga
sections.title: The Divine Glories
sections.subtitle: A catalogue of everything superlative, and the strange logic of a list

blocks.html: Arjuna, now fully convinced and hungry, asks Krishna to describe his vibhūtis — his manifestations, his glories, the forms in which he pervades the world — because he cannot get enough of hearing it: there is no satiety in listening to your nectar (10.18). What follows is one of the great catalogues in world literature, and it works by a rule you can learn in one sentence: in every category of thing, Krishna is the one that most fully is what that category means.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The seed of the list
blocks.sk:
अहमात्मा गुडाकेश सर्वभूताशयस्थितः ।
अहमादिश्च मध्यं च भूतानामन्त एव च ॥
blocks.tr: aham ātmā guḍākeśa sarva-bhūtāśaya-sthitaḥ / aham ādiś ca madhyaṁ ca bhūtānām anta eva ca
blocks.mn: "I am the Self, O Gudakesha, seated in the hearts of all beings. I am the beginning, the middle, and the very end of beings."

blocks.html: Then the list. Of the Adityas, Vishnu; of lights, the radiant sun; of the Vedas, the Sama Veda; of the gods, Indra; of the senses, the mind; of the Rudras, Shankara; of mountains, Meru; of bodies of water, the ocean; of trees, the ashvattha; of rivers, the Ganga; of weapons, the thunderbolt; of seasons, spring. Among the Pandavas — and he says this to Arjuna's face — I am Dhananjaya, which is Arjuna's own name (10.37). Among letters, he says at 10.33, I am the letter A.

blocks.tag: Symbolic Lens · Why the letter A

blocks.html: Akṣarāṇām akāro 'smi — of syllables I am A. In Sanskrit this is not a boast about coming first alphabetically. The vowel a is the sound the open mouth makes when no articulation is added at all; every other sound is a modification of that basic voicing, and in the traditional grammatical analysis a consonant cannot even be pronounced without it. It is not the first thing in the series. It is what all the rest of the series is made of. The whole chapter's logic is contained in that one item: Krishna is not claiming to be the most impressive entry in each category, but the underlying capacity that makes the category possible.

And a darker item in the same list, easy to miss: I am death, the devourer of all (10.34), sitting between "the fame, the fortune, the speech, the memory" and no more emphasis than any other line. Chapter eleven takes that half-verse and makes Arjuna look at it.
Why the List Cannot Be Finished

Krishna ends the catalogue by declaring it hopeless. There is no end to my divine manifestations; what I have declared is only a fraction, offered as illustration (10.40). Then the rule that makes the whole list unnecessary: whatever being is glorious, prosperous or powerful — yad yad vibhūtimat sattvaṁ śrīmad ūrjitam eva vā — know that it has sprung from a fragment of my splendour (10.41). And more bluntly still, in the chapter's last line: I stand supporting this entire world with a single fragment of myself (10.42).

There is a real theological choice being made here, and it is worth naming. The chapter could have said: God is beyond all these things, so look away from the world. Instead it says: look at whatever is most alive in each category and you are looking at a fragment. It is a training of attention outward rather than a withdrawal of it — which is why this chapter, more than the meditative ones, is the reason that Indian devotional poetry is so full of rivers, mountains, seasons, and animals. And it sets up chapter eleven perfectly: Arjuna has now heard the fragments described one by one, and he makes the mistake of asking to see them all at once.

sections.label: Chapter 11 · Viśvarūpa Darśana Yoga
sections.title: The Vision of the Cosmic Form
sections.subtitle: The chapter where a friend becomes a terror, and the war is revealed as already over

blocks.html: This is the hinge of the book, and unlike every other chapter it is not primarily an argument. It is an event. Arjuna, having heard about the glories, asks to see the form Krishna has been describing: if you think I can bear the sight of it, show me your imperishable self (11.4). Krishna agrees — behold my hundreds and thousands of forms, of many kinds, divine, of various colours and shapes — and then adds the line that should have warned him. But you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you a divine eye.

The gift of the divya-cakṣus is the same gift Vyasa gave Sanjaya at the start of the epic. The Gita is quite precise about this: what Arjuna sees is not visible to the ordinary organ, and the perception has to be issued to him. Sanjaya, narrating in the palace, is seeing it through a version of the same faculty — which is why the chapter is one of the few places where the narrator stops reporting and starts exclaiming.
What He Sees

The description that follows is the most extraordinary sustained passage in the text. Arjuna sees the whole universe, with its manifold divisions, gathered into one place in the body of the god of gods. Countless mouths, eyes, arms, bellies; no beginning, no middle, no end; blazing with the radiance of a thousand suns; wearing garlands and celestial ornaments, holding uplifted weapons, facing every direction at once. The gods themselves are inside it, watching in astonishment.

blocks.sk:
दिवि सूर्यसहस्रस्य भवेद्युगपदुत्थिता ।
यदि भाः सदृशी सा स्याद्भासस्तस्य महात्मनः ॥
blocks.tr: divi sūrya-sahasrasya bhaved yugapad utthitā / yadi bhāḥ sadṛśī sā syād bhāsas tasya mahātmanaḥ
blocks.mn: "If the light of a thousand suns were to rise in the sky all at once, that radiance might resemble the splendour of that great being."

blocks.html: For a few verses Arjuna is in awe, and his awe is devotional — he bows, he praises, he calls Krishna the first of gods, the resting place of the universe. Then the vision changes, or rather he begins to see what was in it all along. The mouths are not only speaking. They have terrible tusks and they are burning like the fires of the end of time, and into them — he watches this happen — the warriors of both armies are rushing. Bhishma, Drona, Karna, the sons of Dhritarashtra along with the hosts of kings, are entering the flaming mouths, some caught between the teeth with their heads crushed. As rivers run toward the ocean, as moths fly into a blazing flame to their destruction, so these men are pouring into those mouths to be consumed.

Arjuna's composure breaks completely. Tell me who you are, he says, you of terrible form; I bow to you, be gracious, I want to understand you, for I do not know what you are doing (11.31). And Krishna answers with the verse that has travelled further outside India than any other line of Sanskrit ever written.

blocks.sk:
कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो
लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ।
ऋतेऽपि त्वां न भविष्यन्ति सर्वे
येऽवस्थिताः प्रत्यनीकेषु योधाः ॥
blocks.tr: kālo 'smi loka-kṣaya-kṛt pravṛddho / lokān samāhartum iha pravṛttaḥ / ṛte 'pi tvāṁ na bhaviṣyanti sarve / ye 'vasthitāḥ pratyanīkeṣu yodhāḥ
blocks.mn: "I am Time, grown full and mighty, destroyer of worlds, set in motion here to gather the worlds in. Even without you, all these warriors arrayed in the opposing ranks shall cease to exist."

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · The most famous mistranslation in the world

blocks.html: You have heard this verse. On 16 July 1945, at the Trinity test, the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer — who had studied Sanskrit with Arthur Ryder at Berkeley and read the Gita in the original — later said that a line from this chapter came into his mind: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." It is one of the most quoted sentences of the twentieth century, and it is a loose rendering of the verse above.

The word is kāla — Time. Krishna does not say "I am Death." He says "I am Time." Sanskrit will let you get to death from there, since kāla can mean the appointed hour and is a name of Yama; Oppenheimer's choice is defensible as poetry and he knew exactly what he was doing. But something essential is lost, and it is the whole point of the passage. "I am Death" is a boast of agency: I kill. "I am Time" is a statement about what was already true before anyone drew a bow. These men are not dying because Krishna is killing them or because Arjuna is; they are dying because they are in time, and time takes everything. That is precisely why the verse functions as an answer to Arjuna's despair rather than an aggravation of it. We will return to this in the final section, because it is the cleanest example in the whole course of how a small translation choice reroutes a text's meaning.
Be the Instrument
What Krishna says next is the practical conclusion of the entire vision, and it is the sentence the whole Gita has been walking toward.

blocks.sk:
तस्मात्त्वमुत्तिष्ठ यशो लभस्व
जित्वा शत्रून्भुङ्क्ष्व राज्यं समृद्धम् ।
मयैवैते निहताः पूर्वमेव
निमित्तमात्रं भव सव्यसाचिन् ॥
blocks.tr: tasmāt tvam uttiṣṭha yaśo labhasva / jitvā śatrūn bhuṅkṣva rājyaṁ samṛddham / mayaivaite nihatāḥ pūrvam eva / nimitta-mātraṁ bhava savyasācin
blocks.mn: "Therefore stand up and win glory. Conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. By me alone they are already slain; be merely the occasion, O ambidextrous archer."

blocks.html: Nimitta-mātraṁ bhava — "be merely the instrument," "be only the occasion." This is the most consoling and the most disquieting phrase in the Gita, depending on who is holding it. Read in context, it completes the argument of chapter two: Arjuna's grief rested on a hidden assumption of authorship, that these deaths would be his doing, and the vision removes the assumption by showing him the deaths already accomplished. Read out of context, by someone who wants permission, it is a formula for evading responsibility for anything at all. Both readings have occurred in history. We will look squarely at the second in the section on reception.

What Arjuna does next is, humanly, the best moment in the book. Having seen the form that contains all worlds, he apologises for having been casual. Whatever I said rashly, thinking of you only as a friend — "hey Krishna, hey Yadava, hey friend" — not knowing your greatness, out of carelessness or affection; and however I treated you disrespectfully while playing, resting, sitting or eating, alone or in company: forgive me (11.41–11.42). Then he asks for something that no reader ever fails to understand. Please put the other face back on. Show me that same four-armed form; I want to see you crowned, with mace and discus — I wish to see you as you were (11.46).

And Krishna does. He resumes his gentle human form and comforts a frightened man: let your fear go, let a good mind return to you (11.49). Sanjaya, narrating from the palace, adds the detail that carries the whole emotional weight of the chapter — Vasudeva, having spoken thus to Arjuna, showed him his own form again, and the great-souled one, becoming gentle once more, reassured the terrified one. The friend comes back. The vision is not withdrawn as a punishment; it is withdrawn as a kindness.

The chapter's last verses set up chapter twelve exactly. This form of mine is very hard to see, Krishna says; not by the Vedas, not by austerity, not by charity or sacrifice can it be seen as you have seen it — but by undivided devotion, bhaktyā tv ananyayā, it can be known and seen and entered (11.53–11.54). The most spectacular chapter in the Gita ends by saying that the spectacle was not the point, and that the door is a smaller and quieter one.

sections.label: Chapter 12 · Bhakti Yoga
sections.title: The Yoga of Devotion
sections.subtitle: Twenty verses, a staircase for those who cannot climb, and a portrait of the person God loves

blocks.html: Chapter twelve is the shortest chapter in the Gita and, for a very large number of readers across a very long time, the one they would keep if they could keep only one. It is twenty verses long. It contains no cosmology, no metaphysical demonstration and no battlefield. It answers a single question and then describes a single kind of person.

Arjuna's question is sharp and, after chapter eleven, entirely earned. Those devotees who worship you, ever steadfast — and those who worship the imperishable, the unmanifest — which of them are better versed in yoga (12.1)? He is asking about two genuine paths that Indian thought had already produced: worship of a personal God with form, and contemplation of a formless absolute. He wants a ruling.

Krishna's answer has two parts, and the first is direct: those who fix their minds on me and worship me with supreme faith, them I consider the most perfectly established in yoga (12.2). The second part is scrupulously fair to the other side: those who worship the imperishable, the indefinable, the unmanifest, the omnipresent, the unthinkable, the unchanging, the immovable, the eternal — restraining the senses, even-minded everywhere, rejoicing in the welfare of all beings — they too attain me (12.3–12.4). The path of the formless is not wrong. It works. It arrives.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · Why the formless is harder
blocks.sk:
क्लेशोऽधिकतरस्तेषामव्यक्तासक्तचेतसाम् ।
अव्यक्ता हि गतिर्दुःखं देहवद्भिरवाप्यते ॥
blocks.tr: kleśo 'dhikataras teṣām avyaktāsakta-cetasām / avyaktā hi gatir duḥkhaṁ dehavadbhir avāpyate
blocks.mn: "Greater is the difficulty of those whose minds are set on the unmanifest; for the unmanifest goal is reached with pain by those who are embodied."

blocks.html: That verse is a piece of psychological realism, not a metaphysical demotion. Dehavadbhiḥ — "by those possessing bodies." We are embodied creatures; our attention is shaped for faces, voices, forms, relationships. Asking such a creature to love an unthinkable absolute is asking it to work permanently against its own grain. It can be done — Krishna says so in the previous verse — but the toil is greater, and the Gita sees no virtue in unnecessary toil. This single verse is the philosophical foundation of the entire bhakti movement that swept India for the next thousand years.
The Staircase Down

What comes next is, in its quiet way, one of the kindest passages in religious literature — because it is written for people who cannot do what has just been recommended. Krishna gives a descending sequence of four options, and each rung assumes the previous one has failed.

items: Fix your mind on me alone, place your intelligence in me — then you will dwell in me hereafter, no doubt of it (12.8). This is the direct route: sustained, absorbed attention.
If you cannot steady your thought on me, then seek to reach me by the yoga of repeated practice — abhyāsa-yoga (12.9). If you cannot hold it, train it. Repetition, daily, without drama.
If you are incapable even of practice, be intent on doing work for my sake (12.10). If the mind will not sit, use the hands. Do the work as offering, and you will still arrive.

If you are unable even to do that, then take refuge in my yoga and abandon the fruit of all action, self-controlled (12.11). If you cannot even orient the work, then at least let go of the results of it — the minimum viable practice, and still, the text says, sufficient.

blocks.html: Notice the structure. Almost every serious tradition tells you what the highest practice is. Very few tell you, in the same breath and without contempt, what to do when you cannot do it — and then what to do when you cannot do that. There is no scolding anywhere in the sequence. There is not even a suggestion that the fourth rung is shameful. And Krishna then reverses the entire hierarchy at 12.12 with a verse that ranks the rungs by result rather than by prestige:

blocks.sk:
श्रेयो हि ज्ञानमभ्यासाज्ज्ञानाद्ध्यानं विशिष्यते ।
ध्यानात्कर्मफलत्यागस्त्यागाच्छान्तिरनन्तरम् ॥
blocks.tr: śreyo hi jñānam abhyāsāj jñānād dhyānaṁ viśiṣyate / dhyānāt karma-phala-tyāgas tyāgāc chāntir anantaram
blocks.mn: "Better than practice is knowledge; better than knowledge is meditation; better than meditation is the renunciation of the fruits of action — from such renunciation, peace immediately follows."

blocks.html: The bottom rung of the staircase turns out to yield peace immediately — anantaram, without an interval. The thing offered to the person who could manage nothing else is the thing from which peace follows fastest. Whether Krishna means this as a reversal or as a description of what each stage naturally matures into, commentators have disagreed. What is not in dispute is the tone: nobody in this chapter is being left behind.
The Portrait

The last eight verses do something no other chapter does. They describe, in a single long sentence broken across many verses, the person who is dear to God — and the refrain sa me priyaḥ, "he is dear to me," tolls through it like a bell, six times over. It is not a list of achievements. It is a list of qualities of relationship.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The one who is dear
blocks.sk:
अद्वेष्टा सर्वभूतानां मैत्रः करुण एव च ।
निर्ममो निरहङ्कारः समदुःखसुखः क्षमी ॥
सन्तुष्टः सततं योगी यतात्मा दृढनिश्चयः ।
मय्यर्पितमनोबुद्धिर्यो मद्भक्तः स मे प्रियः ॥
blocks.tr: adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānāṁ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca / nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ kṣamī / santuṣṭaḥ satataṁ yogī yatātmā dṛḍha-niścayaḥ / mayy-arpita-mano-buddhir yo mad-bhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ
blocks.mn: "One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and the sense of 'I', equal in pain and pleasure, patient; ever content, disciplined, self-restrained, of firm resolve, with mind and intellect given to me — that devotee of mine is dear to me."

blocks.html: The portrait continues for six more verses and it is worth reading slowly, because the qualities are almost entirely negative in form — a grammar of what such a person does not do. He is not agitated by the world and the world is not agitated by him (12.15). He is free of joy, impatience, fear and anxiety. He expects nothing, is pure, capable, impartial, untroubled, and has given up all undertakings begun for personal gain (12.16). He neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor craves; he has renounced both good and bad fortune (12.17). Alike to friend and enemy, alike in honour and dishonour, in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, free from attachment; the same in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, of steady mind (12.18–12.19).

blocks.tag: Practice · Reading the portrait as a diagnostic

blocks.html: These eight verses are traditionally used as a daily recitation, and there is a good reason for it: read as a checklist they are crushing, but read as a mirror they are precise. Take one line only — alike in honour and dishonour, say, or free from the sense of mine — and carry it through a single ordinary day, not trying to achieve it but simply noticing every occasion on which it is not true of you. That noticing is the practice. The Gita nowhere suggests these qualities are installed by decision. It says they are what a mind looks like once it has stopped negotiating with outcomes, which is a description of a result, not an instruction to fake one.

The chapter's first quality is adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānām — hating no being. Not loving all beings, which is a state most of us cannot manufacture; simply not hating any. Krishna puts it first, ahead of friendliness and compassion. Consider whether that ordering is an accident, or whether the text knows something about which of the three can actually be started today.

And then the last verse, which closes the loop: those who follow this dharmyāmṛta — this immortal teaching of righteousness — as it has been declared, with faith, holding me as the supreme, those devotees are exceedingly dear to me (12.20). The chapter that began with a technical question about two contemplative paths ends with the word priyāḥ, "dear." That, and not the burning mouths of chapter eleven, is where the Gita's devotional tradition made its home.

sections.label: Chapter 13 · Kṣetra Kṣetrajña Vibhāga Yoga
sections.title: The Field and the Knower of the Field
sections.subtitle: One distinction, drawn cleanly, that reorganises everything you thought you were

blocks.html: The last six chapters of the Gita form a distinct block: analytical, systematic, close to a philosophical textbook. Chapter thirteen opens it with a single distinction, and the distinction is the oldest tool in Indian philosophy — between what is known and the one who knows it.

blocks.sk:
इदं शरीरं कौन्तेय क्षेत्रमित्यभिधीयते ।
एतद्यो वेत्ति तं प्राहुः क्षेत्रज्ञ इति तद्विदः ॥
blocks.tr: idaṁ śarīraṁ kaunteya kṣetram ity abhidhīyate / etad yo vetti taṁ prāhuḥ kṣetrajña iti tad-vidaḥ
blocks.mn: "This body, O son of Kunti, is called the field; the one who knows it, those who know such things call the knower of the field."
blocks.src: — Bhagavad Gita 13.1 (13.2 in editions that open the chapter with Arjuna's question)

blocks.html: This is the one place where verse numbering genuinely diverges. Some editions — following Shankara, whose commentary does not treat it as part of the text — begin the chapter directly with Krishna's words; others include a preceding verse in which Arjuna asks about prakriti, purusha, the field and the knower.
